problem: Learned local navigation policies usually depend on scarce, costly real-world demonstrations (GNM/ViNT/NoMaD) or on RL, which is data-inefficient and transfers poorly (DD-PPO). Imitation-only diffusion policies learn only from positive demonstrations, so they get no negative feedback about collisions. Modular planners need heavy tuning and break down under noisy depth.
motivation: Simulation can produce unlimited, diverse navigation data across thousands of 3D scenes, and it exposes privileged information such as global ESDF maps and optimal planners that real data lacks. The paper's observation is that this privileged information can supervise two things: expert trajectory generation, and a critic that learns from contrastive safe and colliding trajectory samples. Together these give spatial understanding strong enough for zero-shot sim-to-real, cross-embodiment transfer.
key_idea: Train one RGB-D-conditioned transformer, purely on large-scale simulated data, to do two jobs: generate candidate trajectories by diffusion, imitating A*-on-ESDF experts, and score arbitrary trajectories with a critic supervised by privileged ESDF values on augmented collision/collision-free samples. At inference it samples many trajectories and executes the one the critic rates best.
insight: The critic is the key safety ingredient. With identical weights, replacing critic-based selection by random selection drops SR from 60.3 to 53.1 (home) and from 74.1 to 65.6 (commercial), about 7.8% on average. Training the critic without augmented collision trajectories costs 3.0% SR in home scenes. RGB-D fusion matters most: removing depth costs about 10.3% SR and removing RGB about 5.1%. Multi-frame RGB history adds about 2.8%, and the auxiliary no-goal objective adds 2.1% SR and 1.8% SPL. Randomizing robot height and camera view in the data is what enables embodiment-aware behavior: a model trained only on low-height (<0.5 m) data drops Galaxea R1 SR from 90% to 20% because it never learns to detour around tables, while Go2 performance is maintained.
method: Sim data engine: voxelizes scene meshes at 0.05 m and computes the ESDF of navigable area (truncated at robot radius 0.25 m). Runs A* on a 0.2 m-downsampled ESDF between random start/goal pairs, greedily shifts waypoints away from obstacles, and smooths with a cubic spline.

Rendering and domain randomization: BlenderProc renders RGB-D along trajectories in 3,000+ scenes (3D-Front, HSSD, HM3D, Replica, Gibson, MP3D), 100 start/goal pairs per scene. Robot height is randomized in 0.25–1.25 m, camera pitch in -30°–0°, and FOV uses one of two settings (RealSense D435i 69°×42° or Zed 2 110°×70°), plus light, view and texture randomization. Output is >200K trajectories at about 2,500 trajectories/GPU/day.

Multi-modal encoder: N=8 RGB frames pass through a pretrained DepthAnything encoder (256 patch tokens each), and a single depth frame (clipped to 0.1–5 m) passes through a ViT trained from scratch (256 tokens). A lightweight transformer decoder with learnable queries compresses the (N+1)×256 tokens into N×16. The point-goal (x_g, y_g) is MLP-encoded, and an all-zero goal embedding is used for the no-goal task.

Unified policy transformer: shared transformer-decoder layers take MLP-encoded trajectory embeddings as queries and the RGB-D tokens plus a diffusion-timestep token as keys/values. Two output heads sit on top. The actor head does DDPM noise prediction (10 diffusion steps, 24 waypoints). The critic head does trajectory scoring, with an attention mask that excludes the timestep token.

Privileged critic supervision: expert trajectories are augmented with random rotations to create collision and collision-free contrastive samples. Each is labeled V = γ·Σ(ESDF change along waypoints) + λ·(fraction of waypoints with ESDF < d_safe = 0.5), and the critic head regresses this label.

Joint one-stage training: the actor loss is 0.5·(no-goal noise MSE) + 0.5·(point-goal noise MSE), summed with the critic loss. Training uses 32 A100s for 24 h, batch size 2048, lr 1e-4 with linear decay.
Inference: the actor head samples a batch of candidate trajectories, the critic head scores them, and the highest-value trajectory is executed as a map-free local plan.

setting.backbone: Custom transformer diffusion policy + critic head; RGB encoder = pretrained DepthAnything ViT, depth ViT trained from scratch (whole network trained)
setting.training_data: Self-generated simulation dataset: >200K trajectories from 3,154 scenes (3D-Front, HSSD, HM3D, Replica, Gibson, MP3D); 1627.1 km, 452 h and 40M images per Table 1 ('over one million meters' in text). Expert paths come from A* on ESDF; rendered with BlenderProc with domain randomization. No real-world data.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D: 8-frame RGB history + single current depth frame (0.1–5 m), plus relative point-goal (x,y) or no goal
setting.action_space: predicted continuous trajectory of 24 dense 2D waypoints (local planner output), followed by the robot controller
setting.simulator: BlenderProc (training data rendering); IsaacSim with GRUtopia scenes and ClearPath Dingo robot (evaluation); real world
setting.privileged: none at test time (ESDF / global A* planner used only as training supervision); point-goal task supplies the goal's relative coordinates

numbers_note: All benchmarks are custom (IsaacSim/GRUtopia and real-world), not standard Habitat PointNav splits, and no standard-benchmark numbers are reported. The cross-embodiment data ablation (Q5; Galaxea R1 SR 90% → 20% without height-randomized data, 20 episodes per scene per robot) is given only in a figure plus text. In-the-wild indoor/outdoor results (Go2, G1, Galaxea R1) are qualitative. The claimed real-world point-goal improvement is inconsistent: caption says 23.4%, text says 23.0%. Dataset size is also inconsistent: text says 'over one million meters', Table 1 says 1627.1 km. Ablation variants (w/o Depth/RGB/Multiframe/Selection/Augmentation/No-Goal) are in the ablation table and are not listed as separate entries.
results: On the IsaacSim point-goal benchmark (20 GRUtopia scenes, Dingo robot), NavDP reaches SR 67.2 / SPL 62.6, beating ViPlanner (60.9/58.6), iPlanner (54.1/51.2) and DD-PPO (8.6/8.5). In real-world cross-embodiment point-goal tests (Turtlebot4, Go2, G1) it reaches 76.7% SR versus ViPlanner's 53.3% and EgoPlanner's 40.0%. On no-goal exploration it averages 106.2 s / 274.1 area in sim versus NoMaD's 36.6 / 85.7, and 112.9 s in the real world versus NoMaD's 29.3 s. All of this uses simulation-only training.
limitations: Evaluation is on custom benchmarks with small real-world sample sizes (10 episodes per robot for point-goal), so results are hard to compare with standard Habitat PointNav/ObjectNav results.

Only local point-goal and no-goal navigation with no global memory; long-horizon exploration and language-specified goals are left to future work, and the method is framed as a 'system-1' to be paired with a VLM.
Point-goal mode needs the relative goal coordinates (i.e. odometry/localization), and no post-training/real-world fine-tuning is explored.
